National Assembly

Complete Verbatim Report of the Meeting
24
2083 Ashadh
Thursday
Meeting Number- 30
The meeting of the National Assembly began today at 14:28 hours under the chairmanship of the Right Honourable Chairperson Mr. Narayan Prasad Dahal.

Right Honourable Chairperson:- Honourable members,
(14:28 hrs)
The proceedings begin. Honourable members, names have been received to speak during the Zero Hour. A time limit of one minute each has been set for speaking during the Zero Hour. First, Honourable Member Mr. Uday Bahadur Bohora.

Honourable Mr. Uday Bahadur Bohora
(Communist Party of Nepal):- Honourable Chairperson,
(14:28 hrs)
This government has pushed the landless squatters from the riverbanks to holding centers and from holding centers to the streets and pavements. In this, 80-year-old elders, infants, the sick, the disabled, and nursing mothers are suffering, as reported by various media. In this rainy season, they do not even have a shelter to protect themselves. Has the government also lost its human conscience? Should it not be responsible? This is the question the general public is asking.
Honourable Chairperson, the government is the guardian of all. It must be responsible, and therefore, their problem must be resolved immediately, not in 500 days, and proper management must be done. Thank you.

Right Honourable Chairperson:- Honourable Member Mrs. Goma Devi Timalsina.
(14:29 hrs)
(Communist Party of Nepal):- Honourable Chairperson,
(14:29 hrs)
Honourable Chairperson, Indian sadhus have entered Nepal. They are kidnapping small children, demanding ransom, and if they don't get the ransom, they are killing them, smuggling some across the border, and turning them into beggars. A few days ago, a child from Chitwan was kidnapped and brought to Kathmandu. There were five people who kidnapped him. A few days ago, an Indian sadhu murdered a Nepali youth at Pashupatinath. I request the government to show its activeness in solving such problems, not just pretend to be active, and to inform this House about the actions taken. Thank you.

Right Honourable Chairperson:- Honourable Member Mrs. Jayanti Devi Rai.
(14:30 hrs)
Honourable Mrs. Jayanti Devi Rai (Communist Party of Nepal):- Honourable Chairperson,
(14:30 hrs)
Sir, it has been four years. More than 70,000 interest-burdened victims have been protesting. Three commissions have been formed. Talks have been held with the government, but the problem remains unresolved. And today, the party currently in government had said in Janakpurdham during a mass rally, an election rally, that they would solve all problems and that you (the people) would not have to go anywhere. Kathmandu is for enjoyment, visiting temples, and sightseeing. Therefore, they were misled, but the problem persists, and they are still struggling. Therefore, their 100-point program has not addressed this problem. For this reason, they have been protesting from Janakpurdham since today. Therefore, I want to draw the government's attention. Let this problem be solved, let the poor and distressed (..time ended.)

Right Honourable Chairperson:- Honourable Member Mr. Narayan Dutt Mishra.
(14:31 hrs)
2
Honourable Mr. Narayan Dutt Mishra (Nepali Congress):- Honourable Chairperson,
(14:31 hrs)
It is the responsibility of the parliament and the opposition to regularly monitor the government's progress and make the government more accountable. Regarding the government's 100 days, it seems the days available have been spent in controversy, confusion, and failure. The commitment to good governance seems to be limited to rhetoric. The economy has not seen the expected improvement, and the pace of development and construction is slow. Farmers heard there was a stock of fertilizer but did not get it. Youth did not even get the hope of employment, let alone trust. Inflation is crushing the people to the point of being unable to stand up. The government's priority seems to be more on publicity than on the people's problems. Now, even after these 100 days, just as the morning indicates the afternoon, it seems that instead of the people breathing a sigh of relief, clouds of despair will continue to hover. Let the government work with conscience.

Right Honourable Chairperson:- Honourable Member Mr. Bhuwan Bahadur Sunar.
(14:32 hrs)
Honourable Mr. Bhuwan Bahadur Sunar (Communist Party of Nepal):- Honourable Chairperson,
(14:32 hrs)
Sir, three decades ago, in 1994, there was long-standing discrimination and oppression between the Tutsi and Hutu ethnic groups in Rwanda. In the last 100 days, even the genocide that occurred resulted in the deaths of 800,000 citizens. The Hutu rule ended with its downfall and reconciliation. Liberation Day is celebrated every year on July 4th in Rwanda. Should Nepal also learn some lessons from this? Thank you.

Right Honourable Chairperson:- Honourable Member Mrs. Madan Kumari Shah "Garima".
(14:33 hrs)
Honourable Mrs. Madan Kumari Shah "Garima" (Communist Party of Nepal):- Honourable Chairperson,
(14:33 hrs)
Chairperson, the heartless, anti-poor Balen government has rendered the landless, poor, and homeless people, who were made homeless by bulldozing their homes, to starve to death in this rainy season, and has also driven them out of the holding centers. Through the Honourable Chairperson, I strongly and seriously object to this illegal and inhumane act of the government. I strongly condemn and protest, and I want to shout that the government should let the poor live, let the poor live, the day the fear of the poor dies, you will not live. Thank you.

Right Honourable Chairperson:- Honourable Member Mr. Yuvraj Sharma.
(14:34 hrs)
2
Honourable Mr. Yuvraj Sharma (Nepali Congress):- Honourable Chairperson, today's
(14:34 hrs)
Kantipur Daily has published a news item titled "Private Sector Met First After 100 Days". The photo of the Honourable Prime Minister is also printed along with the photos of four prominent industrialists. Next to the Prime Minister is also a photo of Sukumaya Gurung, a landless squatter from the KhariPati holding center in Bhaktapur, in a distressed state. The headline above reads "No money in the account", while below, a tragic situation is described.
Honourable Chairperson, the government's express train seems ready to carry the well-dressed and the wealthy, but the train compartment has a chain to stop it. Perhaps the government is unaware of this. The government, which is disappearing from the minds of the poor citizens, may seem a bit dynamic, but it cannot be called effective. It is said, "If the poor are not oppressed, their desires are not fulfilled; if the blacksmith's bellows are not stoked, the iron will not melt," and through the Honourable Chairperson, to the government (..time ended.)

Right Honourable Chairperson:- Honourable Member Mrs. Rajendra Laxmi Gaire.
(14:35 hrs)
Honourable Mrs. Rajendra Laxmi Gaire (Communist Party of Nepal):- Honourable Chairperson,
(14:35 hrs)
I want to draw the government's attention. The work that was regularly done by the District Coordination Committees yesterday now has to be done by the Road Departments. The roads are in disarray at this time. I will tell you a bitter incident. While a mother and son were riding a motorcycle, the mother said it was slippery, "You go ahead," and when she started, the mother slipped, fell, and died. Today, our roads are like that. Regular work needs attention. Another issue is that inflation has gripped Kathmandu. It must be difficult for the residents of Kathmandu, but it is even more difficult for those who come from outside to live here. The issue of gas, cylinders, and drinking water – this scarcity is visible in Kathmandu. How is the government considering this? What is the solution? Thank you.

Right Honourable Chairperson:- Honourable members, the order of speaking during the Zero Hour concludes here.
(14:36 hrs)
Honourable members, I will now provide the floor to the Honourable Finance Minister Dr. Swarnim Wagle to present the proposal for deliberation on the clause-by-clause discussion of the Economic Bill, 2083, received with a message from the House of Representatives, in the House. I am making a slight adjustment to the order of business.

Honourable Finance Minister Dr. Swarnim Wagle:- Honourable Chairperson, with the permission of the Chairperson, I present before this esteemed House the proposal for clause-by-clause discussion of the Economic Bill, 2083, received with a message from the House of Representatives. Thank you.

Right Honourable Chairperson:- Honourable members, I will now put the said proposal to a decision. Honourable members, those who are in favour of this proposal will say "Aye" and those who are against it will say "No".
Honourable members who are in favour of this proposal, say "Aye".
-"Aye".
Honourable members who are against this proposal, say "No".
(The sound of "No" was not heard.) I hereby declare that the proposal for clause-by-clause discussion of the Economic Bill, 2083, received with a message from the House of Representatives, has been unanimously approved.

Honourable members, the clause-by-clause discussion on the Economic Bill, 2083, received with a message from the House of Representatives, begins.

Honourable members, I inform you that, in accordance with Rule 132, Sub-rule 4 of the National Assembly Rules, 2075, a notice with suggestions has been submitted within the stipulated time regarding this bill.

Honourable members, I now provide the floor to Honourable Member Prem Prasad Dahal, from among the joint proposers, to present his suggestions and participate in the discussion on the Economic Bill, 2083, received with a message from the House of Representatives. Time: 5 minutes.

Honourable Mr. Prem Prasad Dahal (Communist Party of Nepal, UML):- Honourable Chairperson, I had also participated in the theoretical discussion regarding this Economic Bill. I and 5 other Honourable members had registered our suggestions regarding the Economic Bill. In that regard, I want to draw the attention of the Honourable Finance Minister.
4
Although these are general issues that were also raised during the theoretical discussion, I want to emphasize them again.

The main objective of the Economic Bill is to achieve self-reliant, competitive, sustainable, and broad economic growth, create employment, and focus on inclusive development. It is necessary to reduce tax rates and broaden the tax base, impose higher taxes on citizens with higher incomes, and implement a progressive tax system by imposing lower income tax on individuals with lower incomes. The tax administration needs to be effectively addressed.

It is necessary to identify sources and focus on revenue collection, tighten the tax system to prevent leakage, and make revenue sustainability effective. By considering cooperation with the private sector, promoting investment-friendly environments, promoting trade and business, creating employment, and poverty alleviation.

Focus on productive investment in the state's priority sectors, especially agriculture, industry, tourism, and water resources. Emphasize import substitution and export promotion.

Implement programs that directly impact the poor farmers, laborers, women, and marginalized communities, especially in favor of social justice. Implement state expenditure effectively, ensuring good governance and accountability. Modernize digital payments, e-commerce, and tax administration. Mitigate the impact of climate change by implementing green economy and environment-friendly tax policies and advancing the concept of sustainable development. Similarly, effectively monitor the implementation of the Economic Bill and develop institutional capacity. Implement government policies, programs, and budgets effectively.

Honourable Chairperson, we are currently participating in the clause-by-clause discussion.

Because of this, I have some matters to present here. I will present them in this order. Some matters have come up, such as the interim administration of house and land registration fees in Section 53 of the Economic Bill. According to the Intergovernmental Fiscal Management Act, 2074, until provinces or local levels have the means, resources, technology, and office management to collect house and land registration fees, the relevant office of the Nepal Government will collect fees at the rates determined by the province or local level and deposit them into the respective provincial or local government fund as stipulated by the same Act. This interim arrangement was made until provinces and local levels were established, and until resources, technology, and manpower were managed. This has continued, so in my opinion, this should be removed from here, I would like to request. Similarly, regarding the special provision for loss of trade inventory in Section 26. I would like to present. For industries, businesses, and commercial establishments affected by the earthquake movement, in cases where the trade inventory has not been insured, the affected person themselves, with a survey report of the loss, can deduct the cost of the trade inventory and the tax paid on such goods as per Section 17 of the Value Added Tax Act, 2052, provided they inform the relevant inland revenue office with details of the loss within the limits mentioned in clause (a) of sub-rule 1 of rule 39 of the Value Added Tax Regulations, 2053. However, to restore private sector industries, businesses, and commercial establishments affected by this earthquake movement, it is necessary to launch relief and compensation programs, including loan waivers and concessional loan programs, I would like to request. Similarly, customs exemption for some furniture, for trade and business, for bringing furniture, machinery and equipment (...time expired).
Honorable Speaker: Honorable members, for the honorable members who wish to participate in the clause-by-clause discussion on the bill, I request you to provide your names within 2 minutes. I have allocated 3 minutes to each honorable member participating in the discussion. First, Honorable Member Samjhana Devkota.
Honorable Ms. Samjhana Devkota (Communist Party of Nepal, UML): Honorable Speaker, this Economic Bill is as important as all other acts. It is an important act like the Income Tax Act and the Value Added Tax Act. This important act concerns the public more. Therefore, it has importance in every aspect, both internationally and multinationally. The provision of concessions on raw materials is very interesting, but it has also simplified its transfer process. However, the balance between current expenditure and capital expenditure appears to be uneven. This also seems to affect the government's balance sheet. How can the trend of very low capital expenditure and weak capacity in our ministries, with expenditure happening at the end of the year, be stopped? I feel that this needs to be clarified. My request is that the Finance Minister should provide detailed information to the parliament about the three aspects of revenue: revenue, fiscal sustainability, equitable and tax management, and capacity building.
Honorable Speaker: Honorable Member Roshni Meche.
Honorable Ms. Roshni Meche (Communist Party of Nepal, UML): Honorable Speaker, the presented Economic Bill, 2083, while embodying the spirit of economic growth and equitable distribution, has imposed an unjust tax burden on citizens and has overlooked some established fiscal principles, therefore I wish to draw the attention of this honorable house.
First, in Section 8 of the bill, a provision has been made for telecommunication service providers to collect a 10% telecommunication service registration fee from customers. In today's era of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, the internet is not a luxury item. It is a fundamental right of citizens, the right to information, and the cornerstone of digital literacy. This section clearly shows that the state itself will institutionalize and promote the digital divide by alienating marginalized and poor citizens from telecommunication services. On one hand, the government is making ambitious announcements about the Digital Nepal Framework, digital labs in schools, and distance education, while on the other hand, imposing a double tax burden on the primary consumption of telecommunication and internet services is a contradiction and contrary to the spirit of a welfare state.
Second, in Section 15 of the bill, a provision has been made to levy a 3% education service fee on the total amount for foreign exchange facility for students studying abroad. Is it not the state's weakness that it cannot provide quality and international standard higher education within the country? When our youth are forced to go abroad due to our own weaknesses, on what principle is it to punish them by imposing a 3% education fee on their foreign exchange? 
Third, regarding Section 33 and cybersecurity, taxes on international digital companies have been included in the bill for cheap popularity, but do we have the necessary technical infrastructure to track and regulate their actual transactions? When the state cannot even conduct cybersecurity audits of sensitive systems like citizens' private data and national identity cards, how will the government prevent the burden of this tax, brought without necessary preparation, from ultimately being transferred to the shoulders of Nepali consumers?
Fourth, in Sections 6 and 35 of the bill, provisions have been made to impose a pollution control fee of Rs. 9 per liter and a green tax of Rs. 10 per liter on petrol and diesel, respectively. The objective of both these fees and taxes is to reduce environmental damage by companies. Imposing double taxes under different names for the same type of consumable item for the same purpose leads to multifaceted inflation in the market. Is this a just tax system? I would like to ask the Finance Minister about this. I wish to present in my clause-by-clause discussion that this kind of double taxation system should be removed. Thank you.
Honorable Speaker: Honorable Member Meenasingh Rakhal.
Honorable Ms. Meenasingh Rakhal (Communist Party of Nepal, UML): Honorable Speaker, I am about to participate in the discussion on the National Debt Raising Bill. (Honorable Speaker: Honorable Member, the National Debt will come later. Not now. It has not been introduced yet.) Yes.
Honorable Speaker: Honorable Member Somnath Poudel.
Honorable Mr. Somnath Poudel (Communist Party of Nepal, UML): Honorable Speaker, I seek permission to briefly present my views in the clause-by-clause discussion on the Economic Bill. Speaker, the Finance Minister has made some new tax provisions. A 3% equality tax has been added for citizens receiving services in private health institutions and hospitals. I would like to draw the attention of the Minister through you, Mr. Speaker, that some citizens do not go to private health institutions only because they have money. I would like to give an example from my own district. In my district, the Mechi Provincial Hospital, which was called Mechi Zonal Hospital, for many services not available there, we have to go to private hospitals like B&C, B&C City, or Omsai Hospital in Birtamod or other private hospitals. For MRI and various types of operations, almost all types of operations have to be done in those private hospitals. Not only the wealthy, but also honorable members in this parliament like Krishna Prasad Sitaula, Gopal Kumar Basnet, myself Somnath Poudel, and the general public have to go to private institutions even for the most common operations. Therefore, even when going there due to lack of money, we have to pay tax in the name of equality fee, in the name of tax. Although this is said to be for the wealthy, it harms the poor. Therefore, I suggest removing the equality tax imposed on health institutions, private health institutions. Second, some people are compelled to send their children to private schools. I will give my own example. If I have to send my child to a community school, I have to take them 1 kilometer away, but there is a boarding school right in my courtyard. Now, should I leave the boarding school in the courtyard and walk 1 kilometer, 1.5 kilometers for the community school, or send them to the boarding school in the courtyard? The general public is in such a dilemma, therefore, some people are compelled to send their children to private schools, leaving community schools. Therefore, I suggest removing the equality tax imposed on education for now. A situation might arise where we have to compel people to come to community schools and community government hospitals, and in such a situation, we may have to impose taxes to discourage them from going to those places, but for now, I suggest removing it. Third, the VAT imposed on electricity should also be removed. For example, a city rickshaw driver consumes at least 200 units of electricity per month to charge their city rickshaw. Is a city rickshaw driver a wealthy person? They are not wealthy at all, so this has also harmed ordinary city rickshaw drivers who make a living day by day. Therefore, the VAT on electricity should also be removed. Finally, I request the removal of the increased customs rate on gold and silver, from 10 percent to 20 percent, and the additional fee of 0.4 percent imposed on it. Honorable Speaker: Honorable members, the clause-by-clause discussion on the Economic Bill, 2083, received with a message from the House of Representatives, concludes here. Honorable members, I now provide time to the Honorable Finance Minister Dr. Swarnim Wagle to respond to the questions raised in the discussion. Honorable Finance Minister Dr. Swarnim Wagle: Honorable Speaker, honorable members have presented important ideas in the Economic Bill. I have also received a letter submitting suggestions technically and formally. Honorable Prem Dangal has also presented these matters. The names of 4 other honorable members are also here. I have no disagreement with the matters written and suggested here. I can accept these. Because a stronger internal resource base is needed for sustainable development, there is no question of disagreement on this. There is no disagreement that policy interventions are needed for the construction of an equitable society, digital technology, payments, and effective implementation of government policies and budgets. I can accept this. However, the technical difficulty I am facing is that I am a bit confused because it is not clear which proposal, which section, which subsection, which clause the suggestions have been made in. Therefore, we also had a theoretical discussion earlier. During the theoretical discussion, Honorable Prem...

Dangal has presented these points, and I agree. Now, under the direction of the Honorable Chairperson, let us move this forward. If we are to formally attach this as suggestions to the bill and send it to the House of Representatives, I have no problem with that. However, in principle, I personally wish that these good suggestions are not rejected as if they were withdrawn. But it was not specific. It did not contain specific points like 'this subsection of such and such a clause needs to be amended, this needs to be removed, this needs to be added.' Therefore, I see no problem in accepting its literal meaning and spirit. However, I request the Honorable Chairperson to decide how to proceed with this technically. I also wish to address some comments made during the open discussion, mentioning specific clauses. Regarding Clause 43, concerning local and provincial matters, which the Honorable Member raised, I don't find it particularly controversial in itself. Clause 53 deals with interim administrators for house and land registration fees. It states that until full operation, the government will collect it on an interim basis and credit it to the province and local levels. Therefore, in places where it is applicable, it will work well. Where there is no capacity, they will collect it and provide the due amount. The government has a universal presence and capacity. Where this is not feasible, where local and provincial governments themselves are resourced, and have the capacity, expertise, and presence, and the government doesn't have to do it, it will not be feasible, in my opinion. Regarding Clause 26, the issue raised by the Honorable Member Pre Danga concerning special provisions for losses in trade inventory, this is also an attempt to continue some provisions brought by the previous interim government in the context of the Janji movement. Related to this, Clause 27, regarding damage to buildings, furniture, and equipment due to arson and vandalism, we have continued the policy of providing up to 50 percent customs exemption. This issue was also raised in the House of Representatives. A suggestion was made there to provide 100 percent. At that time, I requested that the individuals, groups, and organizations who are supposed to receive this benefit have largely already received it. If we now provide 100 percent, when others have already benefited from a preferential rate, it becomes uneven. It also seems not very relevant from the principle of justice. Honorable Samjhana Devkota has welcomed the current simplified and accessible rates on raw materials, and for that, I want to thank her. The Honorable Member has gone slightly beyond the Finance Bill and raised the issue of current and capital expenditure, which is more related to the Appropriation Bill. I agree with the issue you have raised. Capital expenditure should increase, and the situation where allocated capital expenditure is not spent is a long-standing chronic problem, which we are trying to solve. We hope that some policy initiatives we have taken will increase the pace and momentum of achieving the capital expenditure target of 737 billion for the upcoming year. For instance, we have already granted the authority for budget reallocation to ministries with high capital expenditure by Jestha 16. In the past, the Ministry of Finance had to be approached for approval, and files would take months to process. Now, we have made the concerned ministries responsible. In this regard, the Ministry of Finance has delegated its authority. As soon as I became the Finance Minister, our fundamental approach has been not to view these ministries in isolation but to advance development across the country according to the principle of inclusive development. We have also proposed reforms, including the Sunset Law and the amendment of laws considered obstacles to development. Several bills will be discussed in this esteemed house, so we can hope that we are finally moving towards solving the chronic problem of very weak capital expenditure, which has been a problem for decades, I wish to inform the Honorable Members through the Honorable Chairperson. Honorable Roshni Mechhe has raised some issues regarding taxes. The problem is that the state cannot function without collecting taxes. Taxes must be collected somewhere. I humbly request the Honorable Members, if you suggest where taxes should not be collected, please also suggest where they should be collected. Suggestions in that regard would be welcome. Therefore, regarding remote sensing and other issues, this tax was introduced by the CPN-UML. I understand the Honorable Member is also a member of that glorious party. During the tenure of Yuvraj Khatiwada, it was introduced as a Telecom Service Fee. What we need to do now is increase competition, reduce costs, and facilitate physical infrastructure so that the imposed taxes are adjusted in the price paid by the consumer. That is the spirit. However, if you say not to impose taxes anywhere, it becomes a difficult situation. If the Honorable Members provide alternative solutions, I will address them in next year's Finance Bill. Similarly, there are reports of taxes being imposed on those going abroad to study. Foreign exchange is a very scarce resource. It is a privilege, not a right. The remittances sent by our Nepali brothers and sisters working abroad with their blood and sweat are substantial, and expenditure is also high. We are currently spending over 100 billion annually for studies abroad. This is a privilege. Being able to use scarce foreign exchange is a great facility. Being born a Nepali citizen may have difficulties in many places. Our per capita income is low, and the economy is weak, but the right to easily access foreign exchange, buy plane tickets to a chosen destination, and study is a privilege. I believe it is not inappropriate for some Nepali citizens to pay a symbolic tax for this privilege, in accordance with the principles of equity and progressivity. Similarly, the pollution control and double taxation on fossil fuels have different purposes. One is standard taxation for pollution control, like 1.50 rupees. The other is that the government needs flexibility. When we came to power, after the Middle East crisis, there was a significant price hike in diesel and petrol. To provide some relief, we halved the infrastructure tax of 10 rupees per liter that we had been imposing on fossil fuels, i.e., petroleum products. The state should retain this flexibility. As international relations and the global situation improve, it may be necessary to revert to the original tax rates. Therefore, these should be kept separate as executive prerogative, our discretionary authority. I don't see any disadvantage other than adding a few lines. Honorable Somnath Poudel, we have already discussed this issue, Honorable Member. Regarding education, health, and electricity, I hope to provide the final answer in the National Assembly. If you send your child to a boarding school by paying 10,000 rupees, adding 300 rupees to invest in the marginalized communities of Dailekh, Jumla, Humla, and their public schools and infrastructure does not seem like a significant burden. Because even today, about 70 percent of Nepali children access public institutions; their access to private schools is limited. Honorable Members have raised the issue of equity and come with extensive training on progressive taxation. Based on such a simple principle of progressivity, where the one who can gives to the one who cannot, such a loud outcry seems inappropriate to me. Let's add it... A person who can afford to pay 10,000 rupees for their child's boarding school must have a monthly income of at least 100,000 rupees, right? They must earn 10-12 lakhs annually. We have made them tax-exempt on this income. There is no tax. Although there is a 9 percent social security tax, a revolutionary step has been taken by doubling the income tax exemption from 4 lakhs to 10 lakhs annually for the first time in Nepal's history. Even then, if you send your child to a private school (children of Honorable MPs may also be there), you can get a tax credit for the 25,000 rupees spent on your child's education or 24 percent of the tax, whichever is less. So, why is tax imposed here and exempted there? The intention is to lay the foundation, modernize the economy, and formalize it. We have laid these foundations. This could truly benefit us in 4, 10, or 15 years. For now, we have tightened things a bit here and loosened them a bit there. Similarly, in health, if you spend 10,000-20,000 rupees at hospitals like Norvic or Grande, or at well-equipped hospitals like Mechhi, which was mentioned earlier, perhaps 100-150 rupees would be needed to invest in the health infrastructure of our villages and remote areas. There was a huge debate about health insurance recently. This will not generate much revenue, perhaps 3-4 billion. This year, 21 billion has been spent on health insurance alone. It is estimated to reach 30 billion next year. We have planned to build hospitals with a certain number of beds in all 753 local units. If you say not to impose taxes but want a quality school in every local unit, a hospital with an ICU in every local unit, and a paved road reaching my doorstep, but you don't want to impose any taxes and don't want to take loans, then the calculation doesn't add up, Honorable Members. Therefore, I urge you to provide very creative suggestions. I will reflect them in next year's Finance Bill. For now, I have informed the Honorable Members about our specific limitations and compulsions. Regarding electricity, I have repeatedly stated that this sector, which receives such huge tax exemptions to establish a system, and the utilities sector, which occupies a growing share of GDP - electricity and drinking water - must be brought into the tax net. Otherwise, we will become a very weak state, like a banana republic, where anything can be done, there is no system, no one respects the state, and it becomes a system of unilateral exploitation without accountability to the state. Therefore, to bind it and bring it into the system, we are also bringing creative solutions so that the burden does not fall on the final consumer. The 4 percent tax is actually only 3 or 4 percent because the first 50 percent is free. If that also burdens you, increasing that threshold is being exercised. We have already requested the Electricity Regulatory Commission to increase it to 100 units or 150 units, and if that doesn't work, the current rate is 9.50 rupees per unit.

How much money is there, by reducing 30-40 paisa per unit and adjusting the price, the tax has come and settled. Now this will remain, but we are working to find ways so that it does not burden the consumer, and I hope we will find that solution by July 1st. Therefore, I would like to make a final request to the honorable members that the state cannot run without collecting taxes. If there is too much debt and we are told not to collect revenue, if we believe in those things, those arguments, then we all have to serve without pay from the first day. If we can improve our own daily affairs by saying we don't need allowances, salaries, or anything, then it will be possible, but that is not practical, nor is it possible. I have made this request, thank you. Honorable Chairperson: Honorable members, the discussion clause by clause on the Economic Bill, 2083, received with a message from the House of Representatives, will conclude here. (3:10 PM) Honorable members, now I will provide time for the joint proposer, honorable member Prem Prasad Dangal, to withdraw his suggestions on behalf of the honorable members. Honorable Mr. Prem Prasad Dangal (Nepal Communist Party, UML): Honorable Chairperson, Sir, the honorable minister's response to our suggestions was good. He accepted the suggestions, and he did so from the heart. His concern was seen regarding where to place it. His concern about where to put it is a valid point. Because we have not said to reduce this in this clause, add this in this clause, or remove this. We have studied and analyzed the policy perspective, the views, the policies and programs presented by the Government of Nepal to this house so far, presented to the Federal Parliament, the principles and priorities of the Appropriation Bill, and all the matters that have come up in the context of the Appropriation Bill itself. The issues we have raised are extremely important, as the honorable Finance Minister has also stated. Therefore, regarding the technical aspect of where to place it, I would like to make some suggestions to the honorable Finance Minister. The objective and reason are placed at the beginning of this Economic Bill. In the objective and reason, generally, regarding revenue, tax, fees, duties, fines, etc., where and how they were altered, added, removed, or reduced, all these matters have come up, these are technical matters. However, to lead all of this, to establish the justification for all these matters, and to implement this Economic Bill, some theoretical matters definitely need to be added there. If the honorable Finance Minister expands a little on the role and includes some of those matters, then in my opinion, these issues will be adjusted. This will be very beautiful. This is not just a technical document. It is necessary to further clarify and systematize the tenure of officials under the existing health science institutions, BP Koirala Health Science Institute Act, 2049, National Academy of Medical Sciences Act, 2063, Patan Academy of Health Sciences Act, 2064, Karnali Academy of Health Sciences Act, 2068, Pokhara Academy of Health Sciences Act, 2072, and National Health Science Institute Act, 2074, to make them fully accountable to the institution, and to add clear legal provisions for their removal if their performance is unsatisfactory or if they do not conduct themselves appropriately. Due to time constraints, it was not possible to hold extensive discussions with experts and stakeholders. Therefore, in-depth discussions were held with the honorable members of the committee, the honorable members who registered amendments, the honorable Minister of Health and Population, representatives from the Ministry of Law, and concerned officials from the ministry. Only one meeting was held regarding this bill. I express my heartfelt gratitude to all those who were present and assisted in preparing the report. Honorable Chairperson, with the permission of the Honorable Chairperson, I present to this respected assembly the report related to the Bill to Amend Some Nepal Acts related to Health Science Institutions, 2083, passed by the committee on Ashad 24, 2083 BS. Honorable Chairperson, the meeting of the National Assembly held on Ashad 23, 2083 BS had sent the Cooperative (First Amendment) Bill, 2083, originating in the House of Representatives, to this committee for clause-by-clause discussion. Eleven honorable members had registered amendment proposals on eleven clauses of the bill. The bill, along with the amendment proposals, was discussed in principle and clause-by-clause on Ashad 25, 2083 BS and passed by the committee. The objective of this bill, presented to the Federal Parliament, is to make it mandatory for all cooperatives involved in savings and credit business to obtain a license from the National Cooperative Regulatory Authority, to renew their registration annually, and to clarify the scope of work between the Authority and the Registrar; to bring those who misuse and embezzle cooperative assets under the purview of legal action and expedite loan recovery; to promptly refund the savings of small savers; and to re-establish good governance and public trust in the cooperative system by making the process of asset management and liability payment of problematic cooperative institutions faster and more effective. Although extensive discussions could not be held with experts and stakeholders due to time constraints, extensive discussions were held with the honorable members of the committee, the honorable members who registered amendments, officials from the Ministry of Land Management, Cooperatives and Poverty Alleviation, the Ministry of Law, and the Ministry of Land Management, Cooperatives and Poverty Alleviation. The first meeting discussed the bill in principle and clause-by-clause, while the second meeting discussed the draft report. I express my heartfelt gratitude to all those involved who assisted in the report writing work. Honorable Chairperson, with the permission of the Honorable Chairperson, I present to this respected assembly the report related to the Cooperative (First Amendment) Bill, 2083, passed by the committee on Ashad 25, 2083 BS. Thank you. Honorable Chairperson: Honorable members, this meeting is adjourned here, with the next meeting of the National Assembly to be held today after 10 minutes (at 16:04). (Subsequently, this meeting was adjourned here, with the next meeting to be held today after 10 minutes.) Adjourned: 16:05.

sections.summary_en: Several members raised concerns during the Zero Hour. Uday Bahadur Bohora spoke about the plight of landless squatters displaced by the government. Goma Devi Timalsina highlighted issues of child kidnapping and murder by Indian sadhus. Jayanti Devi Rai discussed the unresolved problems of interest-burdened victims. Narayan Dutt Mishra criticized the government's performance in its first 100 days, citing economic stagnation and inflation. Bhuwan Bahadur Sunar drew parallels with Rwanda's history of ethnic conflict. Madan Kumari Shah "Garima" condemned the government's actions against the poor and landless. Yuvraj Sharma critiqued the government's focus on the wealthy over the poor, referencing a newspaper article. Rajendra Laxmi Gaire raised concerns about road conditions and inflation, particularly the scarcity of gas and water in Kathmandu.
